name: Roaming Regulation
evidence_rating: strong: several peer-reviewed causal studies of Roam Like at Home plus regular BEREC/Commission data; gaps on quality of service
summary: Since roaming charges in the EU ended in 2017, mobile data use abroad has risen about 48-fold, and peer-reviewed studies find large consumer gains (about EUR 2.44 per traveller per day) that outweigh operators' lost profits, with no sign of higher domestic prices. The 2022 recast kept the regime sustainable: no network operator has needed a surcharge derogation since 2022. The main shortfall is quality: a 2025 study found 76% of travellers get slower download speeds abroad than at home.

indicators.objective: The 2021 proposal's financial statement contains no usable indicators (sections 1.4.2-1.4.4 hold added-value and coherence text); monitoring relies on BEREC data and Commission reviews due by 30 June 2025 and 30 June 2029 (Art. 21). Evidence below also covers 'Roam Like at Home' (RLAH) introduced in 2017 under Regulations 531/2012 and 2015/2120

indicators.indicator: Fewer operators with unsustainable roaming margins (reduction of 42% in 2023 and 52% in 2025 vs baseline); users at risk of surcharges under derogations reduced by more than 40%
indicators.evidence: Since 2022 no mobile network operator has requested a sustainability derogation; volumes subject to surcharges below 0.82% in every Member State considered; actual wholesale data prices fell to EUR 0.7/GB in Q3 2024 (-50% vs Q3 2021).

indicators.indicator: Unleash demand: retail roaming traffic tripled for voice and rose twelve-fold for data between summer 2016 and 2018
indicators.evidence: Data roaming up 48-fold in Q3 since 2017; voice slowly declining since 2019 (OTT substitution). Causal studies confirm large traffic and consumer-surplus gains (EUR 2.44 per user per travel day).
indicators.sources: COM(2019) 616; COM(2025) 324; Quinn et al. 2024; Canzian et al. 2025

indicators.indicator: RLAH should not raise domestic prices
indicators.evidence: BEREC data: domestic average revenue per paying user stable 2019-2024. Grzybowski & Muñoz-Acevedo find the regulation reduced operator revenue per user but had no effect on tariffs in the latest phase.

indicators.indicator: Roaming customers get the same quality (speed, network generation) as at home where technically feasible
indicators.evidence: 2025 study for the Commission: 76% of roaming users had lower download speeds than on their home network and latency was worse in 92% of cases; compliance 'could be significantly improved'. Complaints low; about 80% of travellers say they benefit.

literature.citation: European Commission (2021), Impact Assessment accompanying the Roaming Regulation recast (executive summary SWD(2021) 27), SWD(2021) 28
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the Roaming Regulation recast (executive summary SWD(2021) 27)
literature.outcomes: operator margins; surcharges; quality of service
literature.headline: Lower wholesale caps reduce unsustainable negative roaming margins by 42% (2023) and 52% (2025) vs baseline; users at risk of surcharges cut by more than 40%; compliance costs under 6 person-days per operator per year; about 170 million roaming customers
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected lower wholesale caps to keep roaming at home prices sustainable for operators and to cut the number of people facing surcharges by over 40%.

literature.citation: European Commission (2019), Report on the review of the roaming market, COM(2019) 616
literature.title: Report on the review of the roaming market
literature.headline: Summer 2018 roaming data use 12 times and voice 3 times summer 2016 levels; average roaming data use 440 MB/month vs 60 MB
literature.summary_plain: Two years after roaming charges ended, people used 12 times more mobile data when travelling in the EU.

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Report on the review of the roaming market, COM(2025) 324 (with SWD(2025) 164)
literature.title: Report on the review of the roaming market
literature.method: descriptive (BEREC data, Eurobarometer, QoS measurement study)
literature.outcomes: traffic; wholesale prices; domestic prices; quality of service
literature.headline: RLAH fit for purpose; data roaming up 48-fold (Q3) since 2017; wholesale data prices EUR 0.7/GB in Q3 2024 (-50% vs 2021); no MNO derogations since 2022; domestic ARPU stable 2019-24; but 76% of roamers get slower download speeds than at home
literature.summary_plain: The Commission found roaming at home prices working well, with no sign of higher domestic bills, but most travellers still get slower mobile internet abroad than at home.

literature.citation: Quinn, Godinho de Matos & Peukert (2024), The Welfare Effects of Mobile Internet Access: Evidence from Roam-Like-at-Home, The Economic Journal 134(659)
literature.title: The Welfare Effects of Mobile Internet Access: Evidence from Roam-Like-at-Home
literature.method: demand/welfare estimation on individual-level mobile consumption data around the June 2017 reform
literature.headline: Consumer surplus rose by about EUR 2.44 per user per travel day; around 40% of gains from new users (lower deadweight loss); effects differ by usage intensity and business vs leisure travel
literature.summary_plain: Ending roaming charges was worth about EUR 2.44 per traveller per day to consumers, partly because many people started using mobile internet abroad for the first time.
literature.quality: quasi-experimental; individual-level data from operator records

literature.citation: Canzian, Mazzarella, Ronchail, Verboven & Verzillo (2025), Evaluating the impact of price caps - Evidence from the European roam-like-at-home regulation, International Journal of Industrial Organization 103 (earlier CEPR DP16554, CESifo WP 9303)
literature.title: Evaluating the impact of price caps - Evidence from the European roam-like-at-home regulation
literature.venue: International Journal of Industrial Organization 103 (earlier CEPR DP16554, CESifo WP 9303)
literature.method: difference-in-differences (rest-of-world roaming as control) plus welfare analysis
literature.outcomes: roaming traffic; revenues; consumer surplus; profits
literature.headline: Large but uneven effects on retail and wholesale traffic and revenues; consumer surplus gains large, mainly from data, and bigger in small open economies and countries with previously high prices; total welfare rises as consumer gains outweigh profit losses
literature.summary_plain: A study by JRC and university economists found ending roaming charges raised total welfare: consumers' gains, especially on data, far outweighed operators' lost profits.
literature.period_geography: EEA vs rest of world, around 2017

literature.citation: Grzybowski & Muñoz-Acevedo (2023), Impact of roaming regulation on revenues and prices of mobile operators in the EU, International Journal of Industrial Organization 89
literature.title: Impact of roaming regulation on revenues and prices of mobile operators in the EU
literature.method: difference-in-differences and hedonic price regressions (operator and plan-level data)
literature.headline: Roaming regulation decreased mobile operators' revenues per user but had no impact on tariffs in the latest phase (no domestic waterbed)
literature.summary_plain: Roaming rules cut operators' revenue per customer but did not push up domestic mobile prices.

literature.citation: Boto-García & Santana-Gallego (2026), Roam Like at Home: The Effect of Zero-Roaming Charges on Tourism Flows, SSRN working paper
literature.title: Roam Like at Home: The Effect of Zero-Roaming Charges on Tourism Flows
literature.method: structural gravity model with difference-in-differences (world tourist arrivals 2012-2019) plus survey microdata
literature.headline: Abolishing roaming charges significantly increased intra-EEA tourism flows, especially from higher-income origins and between distant country pairs; survey evidence shows more trips and more mobile internet use abroad
literature.summary_plain: A new working paper finds that ending roaming charges led to more tourist trips within Europe.

literature.title: 32nd BEREC International Roaming Benchmark Data and Monitoring Report (BoR (26) 28)
literature.method: descriptive statistics from mandatory operator data collection (Art. 21(2) Roaming Regulation) plus NRA/operator questionnaires on fair use, transparency and QoS
literature.outcomes: retail and wholesale roaming prices, roaming volumes, fair-use policy and transparency compliance
literature.headline: EEA average wholesale data roaming price fell from EUR 0.67/GB (Q4 2024) to EUR 0.57/GB (Q3 2025), staying below the regulated caps (EUR 1.30/GB in Q3 2025 per the report's table); 91% of roaming providers inform users of regulated and alternative tariffs.
literature.summary_plain: The EU telecoms regulators' body tracks what operators charge each other and customers for roaming. Wholesale prices for mobile data abroad kept falling and stayed well under the legal maximums, and most operators meet the transparency rules.
literature.period_geography: EU/EEA, Q4 2020 to Q3 2025 (focus Q4 2024 to Q3 2025)
literature.quality: Official monitoring data, broad coverage; descriptive only, no counterfactual; BEREC notes data gaps from some operators.
literature.citation: BEREC (2026), 32nd BEREC International Roaming Benchmark Data and Monitoring Report (BoR (26) 28), BEREC reports

literature.title: Eurobarometer survey report on the end of roaming
literature.venue: Flash Eurobarometer / Shaping Europe's digital future library
literature.method: telephone survey of about 26,000 respondents aged 15+ in all 28 Member States
literature.outcomes: awareness of roam-like-at-home, perceived benefit, mobile use while travelling in the EU
literature.headline: 69% of respondents believed the end of roaming charges would benefit them personally or someone close to them; awareness rose with travel after 15 June 2017.
literature.summary_plain: A large EU-wide phone survey a year after roaming charges were abolished found most people knew about the change and expected to benefit from it.
literature.period_geography: EU28, travel after 15 June 2017; published July 2018
literature.quality: Concerns the 2017 roam-like-at-home rules that the 2022 recast extends (predecessor provision); perceptions survey, no counterfactual; only landing page read.
literature.interested_party: European Commission (DG CNECT) assessing its own policy
literature.citation: European Commission (DG CNECT), Flash Eurobarometer (2018), Eurobarometer survey report on the end of roaming, Flash Eurobarometer / Shaping Europe's digital future library
